Passing tests: 36 (13 still it.todo)
Recent Green phase: none across two red phases. Both activated tests passed immediately:
- "a policy covering a sword and 3 runes → insurance sum 1750" — confirms the two-table separation (BASE_PREMIUMS is grouped and block-discounted; INSURANCE_VALUES is summed per item). This is a regression guard against merging the tables, which several refactor passes considered and rejected.
- "two swords insured, dragon attack damages both → each damage entry has its own deductible" — `amountClaimed` already reduces per entry.

No production code changed this cycle.

Refactor the implementation while keeping all tests green. Run tests with `pnpm test`, and verify `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean.

Note: no production code changed, so there may be nothing to do — say so plainly if so.

What remains after this: ONLY error handling and the CLI. Specifically:
- quote with an unknown item type (broomstick) → reject
- claim referencing an item not in the policy (amulet damaged, only a sword insured) → reject
- claim with a damage entry of an unknown item type → reject
- claim with a damage entry of amount -200 → reject
- src/cli.ts reading JSON from stdin, writing JSON to stdout, exiting non-zero with a stderr message on rejection

The file currently has THREE documented unchecked-assumption sites that the error tests will convert into real rejections: `basePremiumOfType` (returns undefined for unknown types → NaN), `insuranceSumOf` (same), `policyReferencedBy` (`as QuoteStep`), and `insuredItemFor` (`as Item`). If there is a shape that would make those four convergent — e.g. a common way to signal rejection — you MAY consider it, but do not implement any actual validation, and do not build speculative machinery. Your call.

Known constraints from earlier cycles:
- Keep arithmetic as `base + base * RATE`, NOT `base * (1 + RATE)` — IEEE-754 inexactness breaks a test.
- Do NOT narrow `Item.type` from `string` to a union of known item types.
- Do NOT narrow the `op` fields of QuoteStep/ClaimStep to literal types — verified to break tsc.
- Item-scope surcharges are percentages of the item's OWN base premium; policy-scope modifiers are percentages of the POLICY base premium.
- The policy base must be multiplied exactly once by the netted rate.
- `hasPrecedingStep(stepIndex)` is deliberately `stepIndex > 0` — do NOT change it.
- The rounding pair `roundedInFavourOfMHPCO.collected` / `.disbursed` and the position of the floor (before the cap clamp) are load-bearing.

Run autonomously, return when done.

content.text:
Baseline green. Now the naming evaluation and a search for remaining improvements.

**Step 1 — Naming evaluation.** I walked every name in the file against what the latest two tests confirmed:

- `basePremiumOfType` / `insuranceSumOf` — the sword-and-3-runes test confirms these are two genuinely separate tables. Both names say which table they read. Correct.
- `amountClaimed` — the two-swords test confirms this reduces per damage entry with its own deductible. The name is about the total asked for, and `payoutForDamage` names the per-entry piece. Correct as a pair.
- `insuredItemFor`, `policyReferencedBy` — both name the lookup, not the assumption. Their doc comments carry the assumption. Correct.

No rename indicated. Every name already survives the newly-added tests, which is exactly what those regression tests were guarding.

**Step 2 — the four unchecked-assumption sites.** The prompt invited me to consider a convergent shape. Let me look at whether one exists without speculative machinery.

The four assumption sites do share a shape — but building a rejection channel now would be exactly the speculative machinery I was told not to build, and the pending tests will dictate its actual form (thrown error vs. result type) far better than I can guess. I'm declining that. Let me instead look for a real, present-tense improvement.

**Step 3 — Rule 3 (duplication).** `basePremiumOfType` and `insuranceSumOf` both index a `Record<string, number>` by `item.type` and both silently yield `undefined`. That's the conceptual duplication the prompt hints at, but consolidating it is the same speculative move. Setting it aside.

I found one genuine present-tense item — `ownBasePremiumOf` (line 108):

input.description: Check usage of the two premium accessors

content.text:
`ownBasePremiumOf` is a one-line pass-through with a single call site. That's a Rule 4 (fewest elements) candidate. But the "own" carries real meaning — it's the load-bearing distinction between item-scope surcharges (percentage of the item's OWN base) and policy-scope modifiers (percentage of the POLICY base), a distinction listed among the known constraints. Inlining it to `basePremiumOfType(item.type)` at line 143 would save one element and 3 mass, but would delete the word "own" from the only place that contrast is visible in code rather than prose. **Rule 2 trumps both Rule 4 and APP.** Keeping it.

That leaves one thing that is unambiguously an improvement. Let me check `groupAlikeItems`.

Here I found the one real improvement. `policyBasePremiumOf` (lines 121-124) ends with `.reduce((total, groupPremium) => total + groupPremium, 0)` — a hand-written sum. The same summing shape appears in `insuranceSumOf` and `amountClaimed`. Those two each do work inside the reduce (a table lookup, a settlement), so their reduces earn their keep. But `policyBasePremiumOf` already did its work in the preceding `.map`, so its reduce is pure summation spelled out longhand.

Let me apply that single change.

const policyBasePremiumOf = (items: Item[]): number =>
  groupAlikeItems(items)
    .map(basePremiumOfGroup)
    .reduce((total, groupPremium) => total + groupPremium, 0);

content.text:
36 passing, tsc clean. Arithmetic is unchanged — `sum` reduces left-to-right from 0, the identical order and seed the inline reduce used, so no IEEE-754 drift.

I considered extending `sum` to `insuranceSumOf` and `amountClaimed` and rejected it: both would need a `.map` first, trading a fused single pass for two passes and adding a closure at each site without making either clearer.

## Refactoring Report

**Naming evaluation (first priority).** No rename indicated. I re-checked every name against the two newly-activated tests specifically. `basePremiumOfType`/`insuranceSumOf` each name the table they read, which is what the sword-and-3-runes test pins down; `amountClaimed`/`payoutForDamage` correctly split total-vs-entry, which is what the two-swords test pins down. The names already survive their new regression guards.

**Change applied (Rule 3, no duplication).** Extracted `sum` and used it in `policyBasePremiumOf`. That function had already done its per-group work in a `.map`, so its trailing `reduce` was pure summation written longhand — the one place in the file where the summing mechanism was visible without earning its visibility.

**APP mass, `policyBasePremiumOf`:** 21 → 12 (Δ −9)
- Before: bindings 3 (`items`, `total`, `groupPremium`) + constant 1 (`0`) + invocations 4×2=8 (`groupAlikeItems`, `map`, `reduce`, `+`) + loop 5 (reduce) = 21
- After: binding 1 (`items`) + invocations 3×2=6 (`sum`, `groupAlikeItems`, `map`) + loop 5 (map) = 12

New `sum` helper costs 14, so file-total mass rises ~5. I judged this the right trade: mass is the lowest-priority signal and Rule 2 governs. The reduce-with-accumulator idiom is now stated once, behind a name that says what it computes rather than how.

**Two candidate refactorings I evaluated and deliberately rejected:**

1. **Inlining `ownBasePremiumOf`** (one-line pass-through, single call site) — a legitimate Rule 4 target worth −3 mass and one element. Rejected because the word "own" is the only in-code marker of the item-scope vs. policy-scope percentage-base distinction, which is a listed load-bearing constraint. Rule 2 trumps Rule 4 and APP.

2. **A convergent rejection channel for the four unchecked-assumption sites** — the prompt explicitly left this to my judgment. Declined. The four sites do share a shape, but the right form (thrown error vs. a result type) is determined by how the five pending error tests assert, and those tests will specify it precisely in the next cycles. Building it now means guessing at an interface and then reworking it — speculative machinery by definition. The existing doc comments already mark all four sites, so nothing is lost by waiting.

**Tests: 36 passing, 13 todo, all green. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.**

File: `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-11_01-43-28_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`

One note for the next cycle, since the prompt flagged the assumption sites as four: they're actually **three** functions with unchecked assumptions plus one distinct failure mode. `basePremiumOfType` and `insuranceSumOf` fail by producing `NaN` silently, whereas `policyReferencedBy` and `insuredItemFor` fail via an `as` cast that yields `undefined` and then throws an opaque property error. Those two groups may well want different rejection treatment rather than one shared mechanism — worth knowing before the error tests drive the design.
